title: The Last Game Before the Roof Fell
dek: UConn upset UMass 56-49 on a snowy Tuesday night in Hartford; about six hours later, 1,400 tons of roof crashed onto the Civic Center's 10,000 empty seats.

setup.text: Dom Perno's first UConn team was 7-6 when Massachusetts came to the Hartford Civic Center on Tuesday night, Jan. 17, 1978. UMass was 8-2 and third in UPI's poll of New England Division I coaches; UConn was tied for seventh, with a single point.
It was an old rivalry. The schools first met in 1907, and UConn led the series 47-34 going into the season, but UMass had taken the winter's first meeting, 74-64 in Amherst on Dec. 14.

UConn was banged up. Captain Joe Whelton, the leading scorer at 16.3 points a game, sat out with an injured shooting hand, and senior Dennis Wolff took over running the offense. One publication listed the Huskies as 7½-point underdogs.

story.text: Perno's plan was to slow the game down, and it worked: UConn shut down the Minutemen's running game and dictated the tempo.
The surprise star was Al Lewis, a slender 6-foot-11 sophomore center who averaged under 7 points a game. He scored a game-high 18, pulled down eight rebounds and tried two dunks, making both.

The bench delivered, too: seldom-used senior Mike Armstrong scored eight points and played a steady floor game, and Wolff added 11 points and four assists. Alex Eldridge led UMass with 15; Mark Haymore had 12.

sequence.text: UConn nurses a four-point lead with 8:35 to play.
Seven straight UConn points, six of them by Lewis, stretch the margin to 11.
UMass claws back within six, but baskets by Lewis and Jim Abromaitis put the game away.

Final: UConn 56, UMass 49, the Minutemen's third straight loss. About 5,000 fans file out of the coliseum; downtown, snow has been falling since before 8 that morning and will keep falling until midnight.
With an estimated 8.8 inches of snow on the roof, the storm turns to rain. By 4 a.m., heavy rain is falling.

The 2½-acre roof gives way. The whole span, some 1,400 tons of steel and lightweight gypsum concrete, crashes down onto 10,000 empty seats. No one is hurt. (A federal report timed it at 4:18; the Times reported 4:15, and UPI later said about 4:19.)
Before daybreak, Gov. Ella Grasso is at the scene. Earth movers arrive to clear rubble piled two to three feet high in places.

quotes.text: I can't begin to describe the absolute horror and just to think people were here a few hours ago
The initial shock is similar to a town that has had a heart attack.
The lights and the scoreboard and anything else hanging on the ceiling are now on the ice
It will be bigger and better, and it will have a different kind of roof.

aftermath.text: Every coliseum event through March was canceled, and the Whalers, the building's main tenant, moved their remaining home games 25 miles north to the Springfield Civic Center.

UConn's next home game, four nights later against nationally ranked Providence, was moved to the New Haven Coliseum so the more than 8,000 fans holding Hartford tickets could use them. Fewer than 5,000 came, and the Friars won 57-47.
The Huskies played the rest of their home schedule on campus in Storrs. They won only three of their last 12 games and finished 11-15.

On June 15, 1978, the city's consultant, Lev Zetlin Associates, reported that the roof fell because the 1,400-ton space frame was inadequately braced and the weight on the roof had been underestimated by about 20 percent. Distortion in some of the roof's top members, the report said, should have been a red flag to inspectors.

Rebuilt for $31.5 million, the coliseum reopened on Feb. 6, 1980, with a Whalers game against the Los Angeles Kings before 14,448. Three nights later UConn played its first game in the new building and lost to Rhode Island, 68-65.

legacy.text: The warning signs predated the storm: when the coliseum was finished in January 1975, the city asked its architect to look at a slight pitch that had developed in the roof, and was told there was nothing wrong.

An Army Corps of Engineers cold-regions laboratory, working for the National Bureau of Standards, later estimated the roof was carrying 15 to 18 pounds per square foot when it failed — the heaviest load since it was built, yet only about half the 30 pounds per square foot it was designed to hold.
Twelve years after the collapse, the rebuilt Civic Center was where UConn opened the 1990 NCAA tournament as the No. 1 seed in the East.
